definition: An unbiased, supported opinion of value for a specific property, as of a specific date, prepared by a licensed or certified appraiser.
The most probable price a property should bring in a competitive, open market, with a typically motivated, informed buyer and seller and no undue pressure.
The 1989 federal law requiring licensed or certified appraisers for appraisals used in federally related transactions above set thresholds.
The Uniform Standards of Professional Appraisal Practice, which govern how appraisers develop and report appraisals.
The date as of which an appraisal's value opinion applies.
The legally permitted, physically possible, financially feasible use that produces the greatest value.
A buyer won't pay more for a property than the cost of an equally desirable substitute.
Value is maximized when a property is similar in style, quality and use to surrounding properties.
An improvement is worth what it adds to the property's value, not what it cost.
A modest home gains value among better homes (progression); the best home loses value among lesser homes (regression).
Loss in value from wear and tear, like a worn roof. It may be curable or incurable.
Loss in value from outdated design or features, like a bedroom reached only through another bedroom.
Loss in value from factors outside the property, like a new freeway or airport noise. Always incurable by the owner.
Estimating value by adjusting the sale prices of similar recently sold properties (comparables) for differences from the subject.
A recently sold property similar to the subject in location, size, and features.
The property being appraised or analyzed.
A dollar change to a comparable's price to account for a difference from the subject. Always made to the comp, never the subject.
Value = land value + cost to replace or reproduce the improvements − depreciation.
The cost to build an exact replica of the building with the same materials and design.
The cost to build a building with the same usefulness using current materials and methods.
Any loss in value from physical deterioration, functional obsolescence, or external obsolescence.
Estimating value from the income a property produces. Value = net operating income ÷ capitalization rate.
Effective gross income minus operating expenses. Excludes mortgage payments.
The rate of return used to convert NOI into value: NOI ÷ value.
Sale price divided by monthly gross rent. Used to value small residential rentals.
Sale price divided by annual gross income. Used for commercial and larger properties.
An allowance for income lost to vacancies and unpaid rent, subtracted from potential gross income.
A licensee's analysis of comparable sales, listings and expired listings to help set a list price or offer. Not an appraisal.
A licensee's estimate of a property's likely selling price, often for lenders. Not an appraisal.
A listing that ended without a sale. In a CMA, it suggests prices that were too high.
